title: Why Orbits Are Ellipses, Geometrically
hook: Newton's inverse-square law implies planets trace conic sections. Most proofs are a calculus slog — this one finds a constant ratio hiding in the velocity and lets geometry finish the job.
key_points: Kepler's first law says a planet's orbit is a conic section with the Sun at one focus.
The proof introduces a 'velocity projection ratio': the radial part of the velocity divided by its projection along a fixed direction parallel to the periapsis line.
That ratio is constant, and its constancy follows directly from Newton's laws.
A constant ratio of distances is exactly the classical focus–directrix definition of a conic.
So the conic shape of orbits falls out of the inverse-square law with no heavy machinery.
content_html: Kepler found empirically that planets move on ellipses with the Sun at a focus. Newton showed why: an inverse-square attraction produces conic-section orbits. The standard derivation, though, is a differential-equation exercise — you change variables, integrate, and an ellipse pops out of the algebra without much sense of why.
extra_html: Hyouggyu Choi offers a route that keeps the geometry visible. The key is a quantity the paper calls the velocity projection ratio: divide the radial component of the planet's velocity by its component along a fixed direction parallel to the periapsis line. Newton's laws make that ratio constant. And a curve on which a certain ratio of distances stays fixed is, by the classical Greek definition, a conic section with a focus and a directrix. Two steps, no integration — and the payoff is conceptual: the conic nature of orbits stops looking like an accident of the calculus and starts looking like what the inverse-square law is geometrically about.

related.title: How Orbits Work: Falling and Missing the Ground
related.hook: A satellite in orbit is falling the whole time — it just moves sideways so fast that the Earth keeps curving away beneath it.

related.title: Universal Gravitation: One Force, Apple to Moon
related.hook: Newton's leap: the same pull that drops an apple also holds the Moon in orbit. Every mass tugs on every other mass, everywhere in the universe.

related.title: Why Everything Falls at the Same Rate
related.hook: Drop a hammer and a feather together in a vacuum and they hit the ground at the same instant. Gravity doesn't care how heavy you are — and that fact runs surprisingly deep.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 'velocity projection ratio' in this proof?
flashcards.back_html: The ratio of the radial projection of a planet's velocity to its projection onto a fixed direction parallel to the periapsis line. Newton's laws force this ratio to be constant.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a constant velocity projection ratio give you Kepler's first law?

choices.text: A constant ratio of distances is the focus–directrix definition of a conic section
It shows angular momentum is conserved, which forces a circle
It proves the orbital period depends only on the semi-major axis

flashcards.explanation_html: Conics can be defined geometrically as the curves with a fixed distance ratio to a focus and a directrix. The constant ratio delivers exactly that property, so the orbit is a conic.

flashcards.prompt: What does this proof reveal about the relationship between the inverse-square law and conic orbits?
flashcards.back_html: The conic shape is an inevitable consequence of the inverse-square law — not a coincidence you discover after integrating, but a direct geometric implication.
